article_meta_title: Why a line on the map is not yet a good cycling route — Routecycle
article_meta_description: The data that separates a line on a map from a cycling route a rider can trust.
article_title: Why a line on the map is not yet a good cycling route
article_dek: A navigation engine can connect two points in a second. But a cyclist needs more than geometry to trust that path: surface, access, rideability, and an honest view of data quality.
article_lead: A line on a map answers one question: where does the path go? It does not tell you whether cycling is allowed, whether the surface suits your bike, or whether a quiet-looking section is actually a deeply rutted forest track.
article_geometry_title: A line describes geometry, not the ride
article_geometry_p1: Most routing engines begin with a road graph: nodes and segments that can be connected. An algorithm finds a short or fast sequence through that graph. The result may be mathematically correct and still be a poor ride.
article_geometry_p2: Cycling is context-sensitive. A paved road with fast traffic, a firm gravel lane, and an overgrown woodland trail can look nearly identical at normal map scale. Riders need to understand not only whether a segment is passable, but what kind of experience it creates.
article_signals_p1_before: To turn a line into an understandable route, we organise signals into three groups. The first is
article_signals_p1_after: : its material, smoothness, and condition. In OpenStreetMap, tags such as
article_signals_p1_end: They can help distinguish asphalt from gravel, or a firm unpaved road from a loose or damaged one.
article_signals_p2_end: indicate whether travel is permitted. The absence of a visible barrier does not make a road public.
article_signals_p3_after: gradient, road type, trail difficulty, visibility, and proximity to fast traffic. Signals such as
article_signals_p3_end: , elevation profiles, and neighbouring road context can help. Each is imperfect alone; together, they provide a more honest picture.
article_signal_strip_label: How data becomes a route assessment
article_signal_1_text: Where the path goes and how its segments connect.
article_signal_2_text: Surface, access, difficulty, and the road environment.
article_signal_3_text: A route assessment with a reason, not a black box.
article_unknown_p1: Negative and unknown signals must remain separate. A segment closed to bicycles is a restriction. If its surface is missing, we simply do not know what it is. Those situations need different messages and different responses.
article_unknown_p2: Treating every unknown segment as bad rejects many usable rural roads. Treating it as good hides genuine risk. A better approach is to show confidence and explain what data is missing. Riders can see where a route is well supported and where their own judgement may be needed.
article_quote: A good recommendation does not promise a perfect road. It explains what is known, what is uncertain, and why.
article_rider_intro: Riders need four clear answers: where the questionable segment is, what caused the concern, whether an alternative exists, and how confident the system is.
article_risk_text: a specific segment, not an alarm over the entire route.
article_reason_text: unknown surface, access restrictions, high difficulty, or a combination of factors.
article_choice_text: keep the faster option or accept a small detour.
article_confidence_text: how strongly the available data supports the conclusion.
article_rider_end: This explanation matters most before a long ride. A small uncertainty close to home is one thing. The same uncertainty on a remote segment with no easy alternative is something else entirely.
article_check_p1: Routecycle uses three steps. First, the route is divided into short segments so a local issue is not diluted by an overall score. Next, each segment is enriched with available road signals. Finally, the system highlights the sections that deserve attention and connects each conclusion to a reason.
article_check_p2: The final assessment is not an attempt to decide everything for the rider. It is a faster way to spot weak points and make a decision before setting off. The clearer the explanation, the easier it becomes to trust the route—or choose another one in time.

route_meta_title: Raanitsa — Kambja: gravel cycling route in Estonia
route_meta_description: Raanitsa to Kambja gravel cycling route in South Estonia: 54.86 km with track composition, logistics, sources and limitations.
route_kicker: SOUTH ESTONIA · GRAVEL · POINT TO POINT
route_dek: A 54.86 km gravel planning track combining two bicycle-adapted rally sections with a connector built on the OpenStreetMap cycling graph.
route_schematic: Schematic route composition from Raanitsa to Kambja
route_map_note: Track-composition diagram, not a navigation map
route_overview_title: A strong candidate for the first field test.
route_overview_text: The route links bicycle-adapted versions of the Raanitsa and Kambja sections. About 82% follows adapted section geometry and about 18% is the connector. It is not an official Rally Estonia route or confirmation of current access.
route_stage_1_note: Bicycle adaptation of the SS01/SS04 direction.
route_stage_2_note: Built on the OSM graph with the BRouter trekking profile.
route_stage_3_note: Bicycle adaptation of the SS12/SS14 direction.
route_ride_title: What to plan before setting off
route_ride_1_text: The finish is not at the start. Arrange return transport or a second vehicle in advance.
route_ride_2_text: The gravel share describes the source sections and does not guarantee one surface across the full connector.
route_ride_3_text: Use a current track and follow signs on the ground; the source graph may have changed since the data was prepared.
route_ride_4_text: The length and expected surface suit a gravel setup, but tyres and pressure depend on weather and actual road conditions.
route_check_title: Check on the day of the ride
route_check_2: private-access signs, barriers and bicycle prohibitions;
route_check_3: forestry work and recent road changes;
route_check_4: weather, surface conditions and transport from the finish.
route_limits_lead: This page uses a research snapshot updated on 21 July 2026.
route_limits_text: Names and official source-section lengths come from Rally Estonia 2026 materials; geometry comes from Rally-Maps; bicycle adaptations and the connector use the OpenStreetMap graph through BRouter with the trekking profile. These sources may be incomplete or stale. The track is for planning and does not guarantee legal access, safety or rideability.
